source_text: II. Porro docendi causa certitudo distingui potest in subjectivam atque objectivam. Certitudinem subjectivam voco, quam assensus quislibet actu in mente alicujus obtinet. Objectiva vero certitudo dicitur, quae per se cuilibet assensui debetur: seu, quae ratione habita objecti, menti inesse debet: & quam objectum, ut sic dicatur, jure suo a mente exigit.
english: For teaching purposes, moreover, certainty can be divided into subjective and objective.
By subjective certainty I mean the certainty that a given assent actually has in someone's mind.

Objective certainty is the certainty owed of itself to a given assent: that is, the certainty that ought to be in the mind once the object is taken into account, and that the object, so to speak, claims from the mind by its own right.

source_text: XXXIII. Igitur respectu certitudinis illius, quam speculationis, seu cognitionis diximus, fides non est certior scientia proprie dicta; sed ab illa potius certitudine superatur. Etenim quo major ista certitudo, eo longius ab assensu removet omnem dubitationem. Sed fides dubitationi magis est obnoxia quam scientiae, verbi causa Mathematicae. Nam si quis perceptam habet vim demonstrationis alicujus Geometricae, de conclusione tantisper dubitare non potest. Sed fideli saepe luctandum est cum dubitatione atque diffidentia, quibus fides ejus impetitur.
english: So with respect to the certainty we have called the certainty of speculation, or of knowing, faith is not more certain than knowledge in the proper sense; rather, it is surpassed by that knowledge in this kind of certainty.
For the greater this certainty is, the further it removes all doubt from assent. But faith is more exposed to doubt than knowledge is, mathematical knowledge for example.
If someone has grasped the force of a geometrical demonstration, he cannot doubt its conclusion even for a moment. But the believer must often wrestle with doubt and distrust, which assail his faith.

source_text: XLI. Denique addit nos in primis Beatissimam Virginem laudare & honorare, pro ratione donorum quae a Deo accepit maxima. Quae, inquit, si nobiscum in terris versaretur, magno nobis honori duceremus eam cum Joanne tecto excipere, ei officia omnia exhibere, quae filii debent parentibus, cum facta sit mater fratris nostri primogeniti. Reverenter etiam cum ea colloqueremur, venerabundi salutaremus, & sanctissima ejus monita exciperemus. Sed quandoquidem in terris nobiscum non versatur, nec eam videmus, nec audimus, nec infinitam, aut ubique praesentem credere debemus, quae nunc in caelo versatur, postquam sua aetate inservisset consilio Dei, ut de Patre ipsius Davide scribitur; nos omnibus iis modis & rationibus, quibus absentes jure coli possunt & glorificari, Beatissimam Virginem reveremur & colimus, dempto religionis cultu, qui ei soli tribuitur, qui ubique praesens est, & Omnipotens, & qui scrutatur corda & renes: cujus in eo voluntati obtemperamus, quum matrem Domini Beatam & benedictam inter mulieres praedicamus: idque multis nominibus; quod credidit; quod ei factum sit juxta Verbum Angeli; quod Filium Dei enixa, eum infantem diligenter curavit & lactavit, eique optimae Matris officia omnia detulit; quod eum salvatorem suum agnovit, etiam in cunis vagientem; quod ejus verbis fidem adhibuit, contradicentibus multis; quod post sanctitatis & pietatis exquisitae in tota vita hac temporali exercitia Deo gratissima pie in Domino obdormivit, & sanctissimam animam Deo reddidit; quae in caelis fruitur ea beatitudine quam suis colentibus Deus promisit, eaque in vase illo selecto, pro ratione gratiae hic acceptae, etiam gradibus gloriae, prout Deus novit, eminente. Talem nos laudibus prosequimur, ejus memoriam gratis animis celebramus, de ea reverenter loquimur, eam virtutum exemplar Christianis omnibus, maxime piis mulieribus proponimus, omnesque ad ejus imitationem, in iis quae sunt imitanda, exhortamur. Apolog. pro sanctiss. Virg. Maria lib. 2. cap. 1.
english: Rivet ends by saying that we honor the most Blessed Virgin first of all, in proportion to the very great gifts God gave her.

"If she were living among us on earth," he writes, "we would think it a great honor to take her into our home as John did and to give her every duty that children owe their parents, since she became the mother of our firstborn brother. We would speak to her with reverence, greet her with veneration, and take her most holy counsel to heart."

"But she is not living among us on earth. We neither see nor hear her, and we must not believe that she is infinite or present everywhere. She is now in heaven, having served God's purpose in her own generation, as Scripture says of her father David. So we revere and honor the most Blessed Virgin in every way that the absent can rightly be honored and glorified, except religious worship, which belongs to him alone who is present everywhere, who is almighty, and who searches hearts and minds."

"In this we obey his will when we call the Lord's mother blessed, blessed among women, and for many reasons: she believed; it was done to her as the angel had said; after bearing the Son of God she cared for him and nursed him as a baby and gave him every service of the best of mothers; she acknowledged him as her Savior even when he was crying in the cradle; she trusted his words when many spoke against him; and after a whole earthly life spent in exercises of holiness and rare piety, most pleasing to God, she fell asleep devoutly in the Lord and gave back her most holy soul to God."

"In heaven she enjoys the blessedness God promised to those who worship him, and in that chosen vessel it stands out, as God knows, even in degrees of glory, in proportion to the grace she received here. We praise such a woman, keep her memory with grateful hearts, and speak of her with reverence. We hold her up to all Christians, and above all to devout women, as a model of the virtues, and we urge everyone to imitate her in whatever is to be imitated." (Apology for the Most Holy Virgin Mary, book 2, chapter 1.)

source_text: XLII. His quoque consentanea tradit Joannes Dallaeus in libro de Objecto cultus religiosi. Quod enim, inquit, Angelos caeterosque beatos spiritus adorare, & precibus, aliisque religiosis honoribus colere refugimus, id non ab ullo in eos contemptu proficiscitur, sed ab unius nostri in Deum Opt. Max. officii conscientia; cui uni scilicet, preces & reliquos religionis cultus deferendos esse credimus. Salvo hoc Dei cultu, de caetero confitemur magnam esse divini in omnes caelestes spiritus operis excellentiam, Beatissimae Mariae, & sanctorum Christi Martyrum, fideliumque Ministrorum eximiam sapientiam, fidem, charitatem, sanctitatem denique atque beatitudinem: ad haec egregia in pietatis negotio facta, dicta, certamina, & saepe & libenter, quoties occurrit occasio, celebramus, & nobis, nostrisque pro sua cuique virili imitanda praedicamus: nomen postremo ac memoriam non nisi cum laude usurpamus: quae profecto omnia ostendunt Sanctos Dei & Angelos & homines, a nobis pro eo ac decet honorari, magnique fieri.
english: John Daillé teaches the same in his book On the Object of Religious Worship.

"When we decline to adore the angels and the other blessed spirits, or to honor them with prayers and other religious honors," he writes, "this does not come from any contempt for them. It comes from our conscience about the duty we owe to the one God, best and greatest, to whom alone, we believe, prayers and the other acts of religious worship are to be offered."

"With this worship of God kept intact, we gladly confess the rest: the excellence of God's work in all the heavenly spirits is great, and great too are the wisdom, faith, love, holiness, and, finally, the blessedness of the most Blessed Mary, of Christ's holy martyrs, and of his faithful ministers. We celebrate their outstanding deeds, words, and struggles in the cause of godliness often and gladly, whenever there is occasion, and we commend them to ourselves and our people for imitation, each as far as he is able. And we never speak their name or memory except with praise. All of this shows that God's saints, angels and men alike, are honored by us as is fitting and held in high esteem."

source_text: XLIII. Postea vero honorem, quem & Angelis & Sanctis caelo receptis nobis deferri par est, & divinorum & Ecclesiasticorum auctorum sententia, his duobus totum contineri censet, τῇ εὐφημίᾳ καὶ τῇ μιμήσει, laude & imitatione. Quorum illud prius in eo situm est, ut bene praeclareque de iis, veluti de eximiis Dei ministris, sentiamus ac loquamur: alterum vero hoc constat, ut eorum mores, & quod communi Domino ac Deo praestiterunt obsequium, fideliter ac studiose imitemur. De objecto cultus religiosi lib. 3. cap. 1.
english: Daillé then holds that the honor we rightly give to the angels and to the saints received into heaven is, by the judgment of both the inspired and the church writers, entirely contained in two things: in good report and in imitation, that is, praise and imitation.

The first means thinking and speaking well and highly of them as outstanding servants of God. The second means imitating faithfully and earnestly their way of life and the obedience they gave to their Lord and God, who is ours as well. (On the Object of Religious Worship, book 3, chapter 1.)

source_text: XLIV. In ista autem Sanctorum Angelorum & hominum εὐφημίᾳ, sive laude, cavendum putant Scholae Reformatae Doctores, ne studio Sanctos extollendi, tribuamus ipsis titulos & elogia, quae soli Deo & Christo debentur: neve pedem inferentes in ea quae non vidimus, quicquam eis tribuamus quod per Dei verbum non constat. Cum ergo Scriptura sacra non doceat, nec indicet Sanctos in Christo defunctos rebus humanis praeesse, & viventium Patronos ac Tutores a Deo esse constitutos, nolunt illos ut tales celebrari: nec etiam iis tribui quod pro singulis fidelibus orent, & singulorum preces simul audire & exaudire possint; cum hoc nulla revelatione divina compertum sit.
english: In this good report or praise of the saints, angels and men, the teachers of the Reformed school think we must take care not to give them, in our eagerness to exalt them, titles and tributes owed to God and Christ alone. Nor should we intrude into things we have not seen and credit them with anything that the word of God does not establish.

Holy Scripture neither teaches nor hints that the saints who have died in Christ govern human affairs or have been appointed by God as patrons and guardians of the living. So the Reformed refuse to celebrate them in that role. Nor will they credit the saints with praying for individual believers, or with being able to hear and answer the prayers of many people at once, since no divine revelation has disclosed this.

source_text: XLV. An vero saltem in genere pro Ecclesia Militante orent quidam inter Reformatos pro certo affirmare nolunt, ac judicium suum ea de re suspendunt, ut saepe jam dictus Carolus Drelincurtius, qui censet incertum esse an Sancti pro Ecclesia orent, & istud inter occulta Dei, nec nobis revelata ponit, quia istud Scriptura nullibi clare & expresse docet. De honore B. Virgini exhibendo tom. 2. pag. 106. num. 179. & seqq.
english: Whether the saints at least pray for the Church Militant in general, some among the Reformed will not affirm as certain and suspend judgment on the question.

One is Charles Drelincourt, cited often already, who judges it uncertain whether the saints pray for the Church. He places this among God's hidden things, not revealed to us, because Scripture nowhere teaches it clearly and expressly. (On the Honor to Be Shown to the Blessed Virgin, volume 2, page 106, number 179 and following.)

source_text: XLVI. Similiter Chamierus quaestione proposita, utrum Sanctorum animae pro nobis orent in genere; hoc est universaliter pro Ecclesia Christiana, & fidelium universitate, pronunciat id nullo certo argumento constare: quamvis fateatur nonnihil habere veri similitudinis; & rem relinquat in medio, ut quisque fruatur suo judicio. Panstr. tom. 2. lib. 8. cap. 5.
english: Chamier likewise takes up the question whether the souls of the saints pray for us in general, that is, for the Christian Church as a whole and for the whole body of believers. He declares that no certain argument establishes it, though he grants it has some likelihood, and he leaves the matter open for each to decide for himself. (Panstratia, volume 2, book 8, chapter 5.)

source_text: XLVII. Alii vero non gravate concedunt, & probabile existimant Sanctos in caelis cum Christo regnantes, in genere saltem pro Ecclesia hic pugnante orare: quoniam id videtur plane consentaneum & charitati qua fervent, & communioni quae est inter utramque Ecclesiam, Militantem atque Triumphantem. Sic ea de re sententiam suam exponit Andreas Rivetus. Non negamus, inquit, Sanctorum Ecclesiam cum Christo regnantem, de membris hic pugnantibus esse sollicitam. Sed ea cura est communis, non ex cujusque conditionis notitia, sed ex generali eorum scientia, qua norunt quod, cum tota Ecclesia nondum sit recepta ubi regnant, semper aliqui militent in terra, pro quorum conservatione ac complemento, eos Deum precari, ut ejus regni incrementum semper petunt, non dubitamus. Summa controversiarum tractatu secundo, quaest. 48.
english: Others readily grant, and think it probable, that the saints reigning with Christ in heaven pray at least in general for the Church fighting here, since this seems wholly in keeping with the love that burns in them and with the communion between the two Churches, the Church Militant and the Church Triumphant.

Andrew Rivet states his view this way: "We do not deny that the Church of the saints who reign with Christ cares for the members still fighting here. But that care is general. It does not come from knowing each person's condition but from their general knowledge: they know that the whole Church has not yet been received where they reign, and that some are always fighting on earth. We do not doubt that they pray to God for the preservation and completion of these, just as they always ask for the growth of his kingdom." (Summary of Controversies, second treatise, question 48.)

source_text: XLVIII. Nec alia mens est Petri Molinaei. Beati spiritus, inquit, etsi non videant quae hic fiunt, nec norint singulos, sciunt tamen Ecclesiam premi ab adversariis, & ei proposita esse perpetua certamina. Cumque ex glorificatione aucta potius sit quam imminuta eorum charitas, consentaneum est eos de Ecclesia militante esse sollicitos. In Thesauro Thesium Sedanensium Tom. 1. Thesibus de Sanctis part. 3. th. 3.
english: Peter du Moulin is of the same mind. "The blessed spirits," he says, "do not see what happens here and do not know individuals, yet they know that the Church is hard pressed by its enemies and faces endless struggles. Since glorification has increased their love rather than lessened it, it is fitting that they should be concerned for the Church Militant." (Treasury of Sedan Theses, volume 1, Theses on the Saints, part 3, thesis 3.)

source_text: XLIX. Quicquid vero de eo sit, communi consensu negant Theologi Reformati Sanctos esse & recte dici Intercessores & Advocatos nostros. Quoniam intercessoris nostri apud Deum titulum solus ille meretur, qui potest omnium & singulorum preces simul & omni tempore audire atque percipere, idque habet muneris, ut illas Deo offerat & commendet. Quod uni Domino nostro Jesu Christo convenire sentiunt. Nec quisquam dixerit fideles hic degentes esse intercessores & advocatos nostros, propterea quod alii pro aliis, ex charitate mutua, orare debeamus.
english: However that may be, the Reformed theologians agree in denying that the saints are, or can rightly be called, our intercessors and advocates.

Only he deserves the title of our intercessor with God who can hear and take in the prayers of all people and of each one, at once and at all times, and whose office it is to offer and commend them to God. That, they hold, fits our Lord Jesus Christ alone. Nor would anyone call the believers living here our intercessors and advocates merely because, out of mutual love, we ought to pray for one another.

source_text: L. Nolunt quoque bona quae nobis obtingunt Sanctorum meritis tribui, & per eorum merita quicquam a Deo postulari: quia Sancti, qui totum quod erant gratiae divinae debebant, nec sibi, nec aliis quicquam proprie loquendo, mereri potuerunt. Neque tamen propterea negant, vi communionis Sanctorum fieri, ut bona & pia opera, quae a singulis Ecclesiae membris per Dei gratiam fiunt, benedictionem & favorem Dei, in totum corpus quodammodo provocent, atque alliciant: imo quandoque Deum, hominum piorum & justorum intuitu, impiis ipsis, quibus immixti sunt, parcere, & tempus ac media poenitentiam agendi concedere: quemadmodum Dominus Abrahamo professus est se parciturum fuisse Sodomae ipsi & Gomorrhae, si in ea vel decem homines justi reperti fuissent.
english: The Reformed also refuse to credit the good things that come to us to the merits of the saints, or to ask anything of God through their merits. The saints owed all that they were to divine grace, and so, strictly speaking, they could merit nothing either for themselves or for others.

Yet they do not therefore deny that, by virtue of the communion of saints, the good and godly works that individual members of the Church do by God's grace in some way call down and draw God's blessing and favor on the whole body. Indeed, God sometimes spares the ungodly themselves for the sake of the godly and righteous who live among them, and gives them time and means to repent, just as the Lord declared to Abraham that he would have spared Sodom and Gomorrah if even ten righteous people had been found there.

source_text: LI. Porro ex iis quae hactenus thesibus hisce & superioribus exposita fuerunt, manifestum est nullam hic esse controversiam, An Beati tum homines, tum Angeli aliquo cultu & honore digni sint, & a nobis afficiendi: id enim ultro fatentur & docent Scholae Reformatae Doctores, nec contrarium, nisi per calumniam, ipsis imputari potest.
english: From what these theses and the earlier ones have set out so far, it is clear that there is no dispute here over whether the blessed, both men and angels, deserve some kind of reverence and honor and ought to receive it from us. The teachers of the Reformed school readily admit and teach this, and the contrary cannot be laid to their charge except by slander.

source_text: LII. Praeterea inde patet Scholae Romanae Doctores, cum Reformatis agnoscere cultum qui Sanctis hominibus & Angelis debetur, non sub eodem genere univoco cum divino cultu contineri; ac proinde non esse ejusdem cum illo speciei: nec cultum istum Religiosum esse, proprie & stricte loquendo: sed solum latiori quadam & minus propria significatione: juxta quam cultum qui Sanctis debetur religiosum dici posse expresse admittunt inter Reformatos insignes Theologi.
english: It is also clear from this that the teachers of the Roman school agree with the Reformed that the honor owed to holy men and angels does not fall under one univocal genus with divine worship, and so is not of the same species. Nor is that honor religious in the proper and strict sense, but only in a broader and less proper sense. In that sense, eminent theologians among the Reformed expressly allow that the honor owed to the saints may be called religious.

source_text: LIII. Illud quoque a nobis ostensum, Doctores Scholae Romanae fateri, distinctionem cultus Religiosi in Latriam & Duliam esse Scholae inventum; nec vocum istarum discrimen, prout in Schola Romana usurpantur, in Scriptura exacte servari: Duliam enim saepius ad cultum Deo proprium restringi, Latriam vero aliquando ad servitium humanum extendi. Vicissim autem Scholae Reformatae Doctores non multum repugnare, quin distinctionis causa, Latria divino cultui, Dulia vero observantiae illi, qua creaturae coli possunt & debent, accommodetur.
english: We have also shown that the teachers of the Roman school admit that the division of religious worship into latria and dulia is an invention of the schools, and that Scripture does not strictly keep the difference between these words as the Roman school uses them. Dulia is more often confined there to the worship proper to God, while latria is sometimes extended to service rendered to human beings.

The teachers of the Reformed school, for their part, do not much object if, for clarity's sake, latria is assigned to divine worship and dulia to the respect with which creatures may and should be honored.

source_text: LIV. Tota ergo difficultas & quaestio huc redit, Qua in re consistat honor qui creaturis Sanctis & Beatis, ac praesertim Beatissimae Virgini Mariae legitime exhiberi potest? An scilicet, aedes sacrae non solum possint de nomine Sanctorum & Angelorum vocari, distinctionis causa, sed etiam eo fine condi, ut in iis Angeli & homines Sancti in caelum jam recepti publice invocentur, & variis ritibus colantur; coram iis tanquam nos intuentibus, genua flectendo, & corpus inclinando, thus iis adolendo, cereos accendendo, & donaria varia offerendo? An per eos jurare liceat, & vota illis concipere relative ad Deum, id est, quatenus Dei veritas in iis elucet, & in iis Deus per gloriam habitat? Ac denique, An illos rogare possimus ut pro nobis orent: neque hoc simpliciter, sed ad illos dirigere preces, alio quidem sensu, verum iisdem verbis & formulis conceptas, quibus sunt illae quas ad Deum concipimus? Quod affirmant Scholae Romanae Doctores & Ecclesia Romana praxi sua confirmat, negant vero communi consensu Protestantes.
english: The whole difficulty and question therefore comes down to this: what does the honor consist in that may lawfully be given to holy and blessed creatures, and above all to the most Blessed Virgin Mary?

May churches not only be named after saints and angels to tell them apart, but also be built for the purpose of publicly invoking in them the angels and holy men already received into heaven, and of honoring them with various rites: kneeling and bowing before them as though they were watching us, burning incense to them, lighting candles, and offering all kinds of gifts?

May one swear by them and make vows to them relatively to God, that is, insofar as God's truth shines in them and God dwells in them through glory? And finally, may we ask them to pray for us, and not simply ask, but address prayers to them, meant in a different sense, to be sure, yet framed in the same words and formulas as those we address to God?
The teachers of the Roman school affirm all this, and the Roman Church confirms it by its practice; the Protestants with one voice deny it.

source_text: LV. Praeterea illud in controversia est, An Sanctos in Christo defunctos celebrare liceat ut generis humani custodes & patronos, quibus rerum nostrarum regimen a Deo commissum sit: Et illos habere ut tales apud Deum Mediatores atque Intercessores, qui omni tempore omnium hominum preces sive corde, sive ore conceptas audire atque percipere, Deoque offerre & commendare possint, ac suis suffragiis ac meritis adjuvare? Praesertim vero, An Beata Virgo agnoscenda sit atque praedicanda ut Regina caeli, & mundi totius, ac creaturarum omnium Domina: ut illa per quam mundus salvatus est, & quae sola omnes haereses interemit: Et an Mater misericordiae, Mater & fons gratiae, vita & spes nostra salutari debeat: quae omnia probat praxis Ecclesiae Romanae. Improbant vero & damnant Protestantes.
english: A further point in dispute is whether it is lawful to celebrate the saints who have died in Christ as guardians and patrons of the human race, entrusted by God with the government of our affairs, and to treat them as mediators and intercessors with God who can at all times hear and take in the prayers of all people, whether spoken in the heart or with the lips, offer and commend them to God, and help with their own suffrages and merits.

Above all, the question is whether the Blessed Virgin should be acknowledged and proclaimed Queen of Heaven and of the whole world and Lady of all creatures, as the one through whom the world was saved and who alone has destroyed all heresies, and whether she should be hailed as Mother of mercy, Mother and fountain of grace, our life and our hope. The practice of the Roman Church approves all of this; the Protestants reject and condemn it.

source_text: LVI. Quibus quoque scandalum movent Elogia alia plurima, quae in Beatam Virginem & Sanctos coacervantur, a privatis quidem Doctoribus; sed Ecclesia Romana non improbante, neque prohibente: Ut quod Mariae Virgini titulus Deae tribuitur, quod Sancti Tutelaria Numina nuncupantur: ut in inscriptione illa quam ante paucos annos memini me legere, in Ecclesia apud Trecenses Beato Petro dicata, Petrus, Helena, Mastidia Tutelaria Trecensium numina. Et quod Virgini Mariae tribuitur imperium & Dominium in filium ipsum, & potestas omnia Gratiae & naturae dona sub Deo dispensandi, & quibus vult communicandi. Quod illuminatrix cordium, & rerum causa appellatur: imo dicitur mundum fundasse & fecisse, & quae in eo sunt omnia conservare & gubernare: & plura ejusmodi, quae brevitatis causa in praesens omittimus.
english: The Protestants are also offended by many other tributes heaped on the Blessed Virgin and the saints. These come from private teachers, it is true, but the Roman Church neither disapproves nor forbids them.

So the Virgin Mary is given the title of goddess, and the saints are called tutelary deities, as in an inscription I remember reading a few years ago in the church at Troyes dedicated to Saint Peter: "Peter, Helen, Mastidia, tutelary deities of Troyes."

The Virgin Mary is credited with command and dominion over her own Son and with power to dispense under God all the gifts of grace and nature and to share them with whomever she wills. She is called the enlightener of hearts and the cause of things; she is even said to have founded and made the world and to preserve and govern all that is in it. There is more of this kind, which we pass over for now for brevity's sake.

source_text: LVII. Porro Beatos Spiritus sive hominum, sive Angelorum, non esse colendos eo cultu qui ipsis in Ecclesia Romana exhibetur, dum scilicet, aedes sacrae & altaria in eorum honorem construuntur atque dedicantur, cerei illis accenduntur, incensum adoletur, & coram ipsis tanquam intuentibus genua flectuntur: dum vota eis nuncupantur, & variae fiunt illis oblationes, ac juramenta per eorum nomen concipiuntur: dum denique precibus solennibus ad eorum auxilium & opem confugitur, & hymni illis publice canuntur in gratiarum actionem pro beneficiis a Deo acceptis, & si qua sunt hujusmodi: nec Angelos, inquam, beatos, nec Sanctos in Christo defunctos eo modo colendos esse, inde probant primum Protestantes, quod talis cultus non debuit ab hominibus sine Dei verbo excogitari. Alioqui sine fide exhibebitur: cum absque Dei verbo nemo certus esse possit illum Deo gratum & acceptum esse. Adeoque si constet ejusmodi cultum nullo Dei praecepto & revelatione niti, inter ἐθελοθρησκείας ab Apostolo damnatas merito rejici potest. Jam vero totum illum cultum in Dei verbo nullum fundamentum habere, ex eo patet, quod in universa Scriptura seu Veteris, seu Novi Testamenti, nullum ejus extat praeceptum, aut exemplum.
english: The Protestants hold that the blessed spirits, whether of men or of angels, are not to be honored with the worship the Roman Church gives them: churches and altars built and dedicated in their honor, candles lit to them, incense burned, knees bent before them as though they were watching; vows made to them, offerings of every kind presented, oaths sworn by their name; and, finally, solemn prayers by which people run to them for help, and hymns sung to them publicly in thanksgiving for benefits received from God, and anything else of the kind.

Neither the blessed angels, I say, nor the saints who have died in Christ are to be worshiped in this way. The Protestants prove it first from the fact that such worship ought not to have been devised by human beings apart from God's word. Otherwise it will be offered without faith, since without God's word no one can be sure that it pleases God and is accepted by him.

So if it is clear that worship of this kind rests on no command or revelation of God, it may rightly be rejected as one of the forms of self-made worship that the Apostle condemns. And it is plain that this whole worship has no foundation in God's word, since in all of Scripture, Old Testament or New, there is no command for it and no example of it.

source_text: LVIII. Et quidem quod ad Vetus Testamentum attinet, fatentur ipsi Doctores Ecclesiae Romanae cultum qui Sanctis defunctis apud ipsos exhiberi solet in Ecclesia Veteris Testamenti usitatum non fuisse. Cujus rei hanc rationem afferunt, quod animae Sanctorum tum temporis nondum fruebantur illa caelesti gloria & beatitudine, ad quam post Christi adventum evectae sunt: sed in quodam veluti carcere detinebantur, quem carcerem limbum Patrum vocant. At saltem nulla ratio est cur cultus quem Angelis exhibent, si quidem legitimus sit, sub Veteri Testamento non debuerit Angelis exhiberi. Imo si unquam colendi sunt Angeli, tum maxime coli debuerunt: cum in populo veteri gubernando Angelorum ministerio Deus plerunque sit usus, & frequentes fuerint in Ecclesia Judaica illorum apparitiones: quia scilicet, Deus illis internunciis apud fideles saepius utebatur. Cum in Ecclesia Novi Testamenti locutus sit nobis Deus per Filium, cui & non Angelis mundum hunc futurum subjecit, ut docet Apostolus Heb. 2. 3. Et tamen neque ex Scriptura sacra, nec etiam ex ullis historiae & Gentis Judaicae monumentis, ostendi potest vel minimam cultus publici partem Angelis impensam fuisse, exempli causa, in honorem eorum ullum sacellum vel oratorium fuisse consecratum, ullave festa celebrata, & vel unicum cereum, aut thuris granum illis oblatum & accensum fuisse: aut in publicis fidelium coetibus ullas fuisse ad ipsos preces conceptas, & hymnos decantatos, vel ullam denique adorationis speciem exhibitam. Quin contrarium plane apud omnes indubie constat. Cum tamen nihil prohiberet, imo maxime conveniret Angelos tali cultu apud Judaeos prosequi, si quidem istud apud nos liceret.
english: As for the Old Testament, the teachers of the Roman Church themselves admit that the worship they usually give to departed saints was not practiced in the Old Testament Church. The reason they give is that at that time the souls of the saints did not yet enjoy the heavenly glory and blessedness to which they were raised after Christ's coming, but were held in a kind of prison, which they call the limbo of the Fathers.

But at least there is no reason why the worship they give to angels, if it is lawful, should not have been given to angels under the Old Testament. In fact, if angels are ever to be worshiped, that was the time above all: God mostly used the ministry of angels in governing his ancient people, and they appeared frequently in the Jewish Church, because God often used them as his messengers to the faithful. In the Church of the New Testament, by contrast, God has spoken to us through the Son, to whom, and not to angels, he has subjected the world to come, as the Apostle teaches in Hebrews 2:5.

Yet neither from Holy Scripture nor from any record of the history of the Jewish nation can it be shown that even the smallest part of public worship was given to angels: that any chapel or oratory was consecrated in their honor, any feast kept, or a single candle lit or grain of incense offered to them; or that in the public assemblies of the faithful any prayers were addressed to them, hymns sung, or any form of adoration shown at all. On the contrary, everyone agrees beyond doubt that the opposite is plainly the case. And nothing would have stood in the way; indeed, it would have been most fitting for the Jews to honor angels with such worship, if it were lawful for us.

source_text: LIX. Sub Novo vero Testamento Christus & Apostoli hac in parte nihil omnino immutarunt. Nec ullum novum cultum instituerunt, quo deinceps Angeli & Justorum Spiritus ad videndam Dei faciem admissi colerentur. Etenim hujus rei nullum praeceptum, aut exemplum, vel etiam minimum indicium apparet in tota Novi Testamenti Scriptura. In qua nullibi monemur Angelos aut Sanctos defunctos invocare, ad eorum opem confugere, hymnos illis publice canere, eosque thure, incenso, altaribus & aedibus sacris, aut quibuslibet aliis externis adorationis actibus honorare.
english: Under the New Testament, Christ and the Apostles changed nothing at all in this respect. They instituted no new worship by which angels and the spirits of the righteous, admitted to the sight of God's face, were from then on to be worshiped. There is no command, no example, not even the slightest hint of it anywhere in the New Testament. Nowhere are we told there to invoke angels or departed saints, to run to them for help, to sing hymns to them publicly, or to honor them with frankincense and incense, altars and churches, or any other outward acts of adoration.

source_text: LX. Neque solum altum est de rebus istis silentium in scriptis Novi Testamenti, sed nec ex Ecclesiastica trium primorum saeculorum traditione simile quid exsculpi potest. Non pauci fuerunt illustres per istud tempus apud Christianos scriptores, quorum monumenta supersunt, & qui in manibus hominum versantur. Quales apud Latinos Tertullianus, Cyprianus, Lactantius, & Arnobius; & apud Graecos Justinus, Athenagoras, Irenaeus, Clemens Alexandrinus, Origenes & alii complures: apud quos nullibi legitur cultum aliquem hodierno in Ecclesia Romana similem, Angelis & Sanctis mortuis, vel exhibitum olim, vel jam exhibendum esse: contrarium vero multis & manifestis admodum indiciis colligitur.
english: Not only is there deep silence about these things in the writings of the New Testament; nothing of the kind can be extracted from the church's tradition of the first three centuries either.

There were many distinguished Christian writers in that period whose works survive and are in people's hands: among the Latins, Tertullian, Cyprian, Lactantius, and Arnobius; among the Greeks, Justin, Athenagoras, Irenaeus, Clement of Alexandria, Origen, and many others. Nowhere in them do we read that any worship like that of the present Roman Church was once given, or is now to be given, to angels and dead saints. On the contrary, many quite obvious signs point the other way.

source_text: LXI. Primo enim, qui secundo & tertio post Christum saeculo vixerunt scriptores Ecclesiastici, in ea plerique fuerunt sententia, omnium fidelium, etiam sanctissimorum, animas certis extra caelum locis, ad supremum judicii diem contineri, neque ante receptum ex resurrectione corpus in patriam illam caelestem admitti. Eorum quidem nonnulli, ex singulari quadam praerogativa, specialem locum Martyribus assignant, paradisum scilicet, ut vocant. Sed eo nomine minime designant caelum ipsum summum, in quo Martyres Dominum videant facie ad faciem: verum regionem quandam subcaelestem, sinu quidem Abrahae, in quo reliquorum piorum animae requiescunt, laetiorem & amoeniorem, non tamen caelestis gloriae capacem: ut adversus Cardinales Bellarminum atque Perronium, fuse demonstrat inclytae memoriae Joannes Dallaeus. Unde patet primis illis Christianismi saeculis, nondum ut traditionem Apostolicam receptum fuisse dogma de illo Sanctorum cultu & invocatione, qui in Ecclesia Romana jam obtinet. Etenim cultus ille nititur hypothesi de Sanctorum gloria & Beatitudine summa. Ad quam cum non admitterentur, juxta Scholam Romanam, Sanctorum animae ante Christi adventum, ideo fatentur illos nondum fuisse solenniter cultos & invocatos. De poenis & satisfactionibus lib. 5. cap. 3. 4. 5. & 6. Et De Objecto cultus Religiosi lib. 3. cap. 22.
english: First, most of the church writers who lived in the second and third centuries after Christ held that the souls of all believers, even the holiest, are kept in certain places outside heaven until the last day of judgment and are not admitted to the heavenly homeland until they receive their bodies back at the resurrection.

Some of them, it is true, give the martyrs a special place by a unique privilege, namely paradise, as they call it. But by that name they by no means mean the highest heaven itself, where the martyrs would see the Lord face to face. They mean a region below heaven, happier and more pleasant, indeed, than Abraham's bosom, where the souls of the other godly rest, yet not capable of heavenly glory. John Daillé, of renowned memory, shows this at length against Cardinals Bellarmine and Perron.

It follows that in those first centuries of Christianity the doctrine of the worship and invocation of saints now prevailing in the Roman Church had not yet been received as apostolic tradition. That worship rests on the assumption that the saints enjoy the highest glory and blessedness. Since, according to the Roman school, the souls of the saints were not admitted to that glory before Christ's coming, they admit that the saints were not yet solemnly worshiped and invoked. (On Punishments and Satisfactions, book 5, chapters 3 to 6; and On the Object of Religious Worship, book 3, chapter 22.)

source_text: LXII. Deinde ex vetustissimis quae supersunt Liturgiis constat, veteres illos Christianos obtulisse Deo preces & supplicationes pro omnibus omnino mortuis, etiam pro Sanctissimis, pro Martyribus, pro Apostolis, adeoque pro ipsa Deipara Virgine. Pro quibus a Deo petunt in Liturgiis illis ut eos requiescere faciat in regione viventium, & largiatur iis promissionum suarum bona, & praestet requiem bonamque memoriam: non vero, simpliciter, ut frustra contendit Bellarminus, pro iis gratiarum actiones offerunt. Jam vero ex quo publice receptus est Religiosus Sanctorum cultus & invocatio, tanquam oraculum illud Augustini habitum est, Injuriam facere Martyri qui orat pro Martyre. Nec unquam aliquis in animum inducet ut utatur solenni illa invocatione, quam Sanctis cum Christo regnantibus deberi docet Ecclesia Romana, apud eos quos opus sit precibus nostris Deo commendari.
english: Second, the oldest surviving liturgies show that those early Christians offered prayers and supplications to God for absolutely all the dead, even for the holiest, for the martyrs, for the apostles, and even for the Virgin Mother of God herself. In those liturgies they ask God to give them rest in the land of the living, to grant them the good things he has promised, and to give them rest and a good remembrance. They are not simply offering thanks for them, as Bellarmine vainly argues.

But ever since the religious worship and invocation of the saints was publicly received, Augustine's saying has been treated almost as an oracle: "He wrongs a martyr who prays for a martyr." And no one will ever bring himself to use the solemn invocation that the Roman Church teaches is owed to the saints reigning with Christ toward people who need to be commended to God by our prayers.

source_text: LXIII. Praeterea cum Gentium sapientes unum tantum summum Deum agnoscere se profiterentur, alios vero quos Deos vocabant unici illius summi numinis esse Ministros, & secundo solum post eum loco coli: ac Christianis objicerent quod supremi illius Dei cultu contenti, negligerent inferiores sub illo potestates, quibus tamen sua quoque veneratio debetur: veteres illi Christiani bona fide agnoverunt se revera tantum unum summum Deum colere, idque tanquam legitimum & rectum defenderunt; nec vel minimam cultus religiosi partem ipsis bonis & Sanctis Dei Ministris debitam esse concesserunt, aut cultum Religiosum in summum & subalternum, vel absolutum atque relativum distinxerunt: Quod tamen ab ipsis postulabat candor, charitas, atque prudentia, si de Sanctorum & Angelorum cultu idem cum hodierna Ecclesia Romana sensissent.
english: Further, the pagan philosophers professed to acknowledge only one supreme God and said that the others they called gods were servants of that one supreme deity, worshiped only in second place after him. They charged the Christians with being content to worship the supreme God and neglecting the lesser powers under him, to whom, they said, a veneration of their own was also due.

Those early Christians frankly admitted that they did in fact worship only one supreme God, and they defended this as lawful and right. They did not grant that even the smallest part of religious worship was owed to God's good and holy servants, nor did they divide religious worship into supreme and subordinate, or absolute and relative. Yet honesty, charity, and prudence would have required exactly that of them if they had held the same view of the worship of saints and angels as the present Roman Church.

source_text: LXIV. Nam ad istam Ethnicorum criminationem sic cum Arnobio respondent. Ad cultum divinitatis obeundum satis est nobis Deus primus, pater rerum ac Dominus, constitutor, moderatorque cunctorum. In hoc omne quod colendum est colimus, quod adorare convenit adoramus, quod obsequium venerationis exposcit, venerationibus promeremur. Cum enim divinitatis ipsius teneamus caput, a quo ipsa divinitas divinorum omnium, quaecunque sunt, ducitur, supervacuum putamus personas ire per singulas, cum & ipsi qui sint, & quae habeant nomina nesciamus, & cujus sint praeterea numeri, neque liquidum, neque comprehensum, neque exploratum habere possimus. Quod postea illustrat illa ipsa ab aulis principum allata similitudine quam eadem hac in re Ethnici usurpabant. Atque, inquit, ut in terrestribus regnis necessitate nulla compellimur, regalibus in familiis constitutos nominatim cum principibus adorare, sed in Regum ipsorum cultu quicquid illis annexum est tacita vi se sentit honorificentia comprehendi; non alia ratione quicunque hi dii sunt, quos esse nobis proponitis, si sunt progenies regia, & principali oriuntur e capite, etiamsi nullos accipiant a nobis nominatim cultus, intelligunt se tamen honorari communiter cum suo Rege, atque in illius venerationibus contineri. Arnob. contra gentes lib. 3. init.
english: To this pagan charge the early Christians answered with Arnobius: "For the duty of worshiping the divine, the first God is enough for us, the Father of all things and their Lord, the founder and ruler of everything. In him we worship all that is to be worshiped; we adore what it is right to adore; and what calls for the homage of veneration we honor with our veneration."

"Since we hold fast to the head of divinity itself, from which the divinity of all divine beings, whatever they are, is derived, we think it pointless to go through them person by person. We do not know who they are or what names they have, and we cannot have any clear, firm, or tested knowledge of how many of them there are."

He then illustrates this with the very comparison from princes' courts that the pagans used on this point: "In earthly kingdoms no necessity forces us to pay homage by name to the members of the royal family along with the princes. In the honor paid to the kings themselves, everything connected with them feels itself silently included. In the same way, whoever these gods are whom you set before us, if they are royal offspring sprung from the sovereign head, they understand that, even if they receive no worship from us by name, they are honored together with their king and included in the veneration given to him." (Arnobius, Against the Nations, book 3, beginning.)

source_text: LXV. Quibus congruunt quae docet Origenes simile tractans argumentum. Nam Celso contendenti nunquam quidem a Dei cultu deficiendum esse & animam in illum intentam esse debere in omni opere & cogitatione, verum id non obstare quominus placandae propitiandaeque sint variae potestates sub Deo constitutae, idque ad summi numinis honorem redundare, Respondet insignis ille veteris Ecclesiae Doctor, Ad hoc ut Angeli Dei nobis propitii sint, & pro nobis omnia faciant, sufficit & noster primo in Deum affectus, nostraque dispositio, quantum quidem humana natura valet, imitans ipsorum Angelorum Deum imitantium judicium, & secundo Filii Dei verbique pro nostra virili apprehensio. Item, Unus nobis est placandus Deus universorum Dominus, & hunc ut propitium habeamus, orandum est, qui pietate & omni virtute propitiatur. Sin & post hunc supra omnes Deum aliquos alios propitios velit, cogitet quod sicut moto corpore umbra quoque ipsius movetur; ita cum aliquis summum Deum habet propitium, sequitur ut propitios habeat omnes ejus amicos, Angelos, animas, spiritus; sentiunt enim qui sint favore Dei digni, quibus non ipsi solum bene volunt; verum etiam cum iis, qui Deum colere volunt, operam jungunt, eumque placant, & una nobiscum precantur & postulant; ita ut audeamus dicere hominibus, qui cum firmo animi proposito meliora eligunt, ac sequuntur, quoties ii Deum precantur, innumerabiles potestates sacras una cum iis non vocatas precari, fragili ac mortali nostro generi se una socias praebentes, ac ut sic dicam concertantes, & nobis in hoc agone collaborantes. Contra Celsum lib. 5. Contra eundem Celsum lib. 8.
english: Origen teaches the same when he deals with a similar argument. Celsus had argued that one must never fall away from the worship of God and that the soul must be intent on him in every action and thought, but that this did not prevent the various powers set under God from being appeased and won over, since this too redounds to the honor of the supreme deity.

That distinguished teacher of the ancient Church replies: "For the angels of God to be well disposed toward us and to do everything for us, it is enough, first, that we love God and that our disposition, as far as human nature can, imitates the judgment of the angels themselves, who imitate God; and second, that we lay hold of the Son of God, the Word, as far as we are able."

And again: "There is one God whom we must win over, the Lord of all things, and to have him favorable we must pray to him; he is won over by godliness and every virtue. But if anyone also wants others besides him, God above all, to be favorable, let him consider that, as the shadow moves when the body moves, so when someone has the supreme God favorable, it follows that he has all God's friends favorable too: angels, souls, and spirits."

"For they perceive who are worthy of God's favor. They not only wish such people well but also work alongside those who want to worship God; they seek his favor and pray and plead together with us. So we dare to say that whenever people who have firmly resolved to choose and follow what is better pray to God, countless holy powers pray with them uncalled, offering themselves as companions to our frail and mortal race, contending, so to speak, at our side and laboring with us in this struggle." (Against Celsus, book 5; and Against Celsus, book 8.)

source_text: LXVI. Ubi valde notandum est quod dicit Origenes, innumerabiles potestates sacras, quo nomine Angelos & Spiritus Beatos designat, una cum iis qui Deum colere volunt, precari quidem, sed ἀκλήτους, non vocatas. Nec enim solum in genere docet unum Deum esse adorandum, & religiose colendum indivisibiliter & inseparabiliter, sed etiam preces nostras ad eum solum dirigendas esse, nec ulla precationis & invocationis specie erga Beatos Angelos, aut alias quascunque creaturas utendum. Apage, inquit, hoc Celsi consilium jubentis orari daemonas (id est, Spiritus qui summo Deo ministrant, ex Platonicorum more atque loquendi usu) qui ne tantillum quidem audiendus est. Soli enim Deo Optimo Maximo preces offerendae sunt; Et vero unigenito Dei verbo, primogenito creaturae totius offerendae, qui ut Pontifex rogandus est, ut nostram, quae ad eum pervenit, orationem perferat ad Deum suum & Deum nostrum, Patrem suum, & Patrem nostrum. Eodem contra Celsum lib. 8. Ejusdem vero operis libro quinto, Omnem, inquit, precationem, atque orationem, omnem obsecrationem, & gratiarum actionem Deo summo rerum omnium Domino, per vivum verbum, Deumque, Pontificem qui supra omnes Angelos est, emittere, seu deferre decet. Ipsum autem etiam verbum orabimus, & interpellabimus, & gratias ei agemus, precesque etiam offeremus, si modo intelligere possimus propriam & Catachrestice dictam precandi rationem. Angelos enim a nobis, qui eorum scientiam, sive notitiam, rem scilicet supra homines constitutam minime accepimus, invocari, a ratione alienum est. Et ut demus, eorum notitiam, quae mirabilis & arcana est, comprehendi, haec ipsa notitia eorum naturam, & quibus, vel ad quae singuli praefecti atque ordinati sint demonstrans, prohibebit ne audeamus ullum alium precari, quam Dominum qui est supra omnia, quique abunde ad omnia sufficit, per servatorem nostrum Dei filium.
english: Here it should be carefully noted that Origen says the countless holy powers, by which he means the angels and blessed spirits, do pray together with those who want to worship God, but uncalled, without being summoned. He teaches not only in general that one God is to be adored and religiously worshiped, undivided and inseparable, but also that our prayers are to be directed to him alone, and that no kind of prayer or invocation is to be used toward the blessed angels or any other creatures whatever.

"Away," he says, "with this advice of Celsus, who bids us pray to daemons" (that is, in the Platonists' usage, spirits who serve the supreme God); "he is not to be listened to in the least. Prayers are to be offered to God, best and greatest, alone; and also to the only-begotten Word of God, the firstborn of all creation, who as High Priest is to be asked to carry our prayer, when it reaches him, to his God and our God, his Father and our Father." (Against Celsus, book 8.)

In book 5 of the same work he says: "It is fitting to send up every supplication, prayer, entreaty, and thanksgiving to the supreme God, the Lord of all things, through the living Word and God, the High Priest who is above all angels. We will also pray to the Word himself, entreat him, give him thanks, and offer him prayers, provided we can understand the difference between prayer in the proper sense and prayer in a loose sense."

"For it is contrary to reason that angels should be invoked by us, since we have by no means received knowledge of them; that is something beyond human reach. And even granting that knowledge of them, wonderful and hidden as it is, could be grasped, that very knowledge, by showing their nature and over whom or what each of them is set and appointed, will forbid us to dare pray to anyone but the Lord who is over all and amply sufficient for all things, through our Savior, the Son of God."

source_text: LXVII. Hic etiam observandum est Origenem, ut multos alios illius aevi Scholae Christianae Doctores, existimasse Solem, Lunam, & reliqua Sydera esse animantia quaedam rationalia, & virtute praedita, & cognitionis lumine illustrata a sapientia illa quae est splendor aeterni luminis: nec eum ullo modo repugnare Celso illos praedicanti, tanquam illustrissimos rerum superiorum praecones, ac vere caelestes Angelos, ipsique plene persuasum fuisse, quod Sol, Luna, & Stellae preces Deo offerrent rerum omnium Domino per unigenitum ejus. Proinde si aliquo religionis cultu, ex Origenis mente, digni sint Angeli Dei, eo quoque par est dignum existimari Solem, Lunam, & Astra. Et tamen querente Celso quod Judaei Solem, Lunam, & Planetas non colant, non solum in genere negat fas esse creaturas illas σέβειν καὶ προσκυνεῖν, colere atque adorare; sed etiam asserit illicitum esse illis supplicare, & hymnos canere. Judicamus, inquit, non decere eos precari qui ipsi precantur. Quin addit Solem & sydera ipsa ita velle, nosque ad Deum, quem ipsa precantur, remittere potius quam ad seipsa dejicere ac demittere, vel eam quam habemus precandi potestatem a Deo dividere, & aliquam ejus partem etiam sibiipsis sumere. Et postea subjungit, Cum Dominus ubique nobiscum & prope nos adsit, absurdum esse quaerere eum precari, qui non ad omnia usque pertingit, Solem, & Lunam, vel aliam aliquam Stellam. Ac denique Celso scribenti eo nos magnum Deum magis colere videri, si & Soli hymnos canamus, Respondet se contrarium scire. Hymnos enim, inquit, in solum Deum universorum Dominum dicimus, & in unigenitum ejus Deum verbum. Adversus Celsum lib. 5.
english: It should also be noted here that Origen, like many other teachers of the Christian school in that age, thought the sun, the moon, and the other stars were rational living beings, endowed with virtue and enlightened with the light of knowledge by the Wisdom that is the radiance of eternal light. He does not oppose Celsus at all when Celsus praises them as the most glorious heralds of things above and truly heavenly angels, and he himself was fully convinced that the sun, moon, and stars offer prayers to God, the Lord of all things, through his only-begotten Son.

So if, in Origen's view, God's angels deserve some religious worship, the sun, moon, and stars ought by the same reasoning to be thought worthy of it as well. Yet when Celsus complains that the Jews do not worship the sun, moon, and planets, Origen not only denies in general that it is right to revere and bow down to those creatures, that is, to worship and adore them; he also declares it unlawful to make supplication to them or sing hymns to them. "We judge," he says, "that it is not fitting to pray to those who themselves pray."

He adds that the sun and the stars themselves want it so: they would rather send us on to God, to whom they themselves pray, than draw us down to themselves, or split off from God the power of prayer we have and take part of it for themselves. Later he adds that since the Lord is everywhere with us and near us, it is absurd to seek to pray to something that does not reach to all things, whether the sun, the moon, or any other star.

Finally, when Celsus writes that we would seem to honor the great God more if we also sang hymns to the sun, he answers that he knows the opposite is true: "We sing hymns to the only God, the Lord of all things, and to his only-begotten, God the Word." (Against Celsus, book 5.)

source_text: LXVIII. Neque est quod quis dicat cum Cardinali Perronio, quum negat Origenes Angelos precandos & invocandos esse, illum agere de Oratione quam absolutam vocant, non vero de ea quae Relativa dicitur, qua sola apud Angelos utendum esse docet Schola Romana. Etenim Celsus ipse, adversus quem agit Origenes, non existimabat Angelos, sive ut loquitur cum Platone, daemonas colendos esse cultu summo & absoluto, sed eo qui ad Deum summum, cujus ministri essent, referretur. Adeoque contra Christianos invocandos illos esse contendebat non absoluta quadam precatione, quasi primi & summi essent bonorum largitores, sed relativa solum, ut eorum sub Deo summo impetratores & administratores. Ac proinde cum Origenes neget illos invocandos esse, qua ratione Celsus, & alii sapientes Ethnicorum volebant, planum est, juxta Origenem, nec absoluta, neque relativa invocatione licitum esse apud illos uti. Adde quod Origenes dicens illos pro nobis precari ἀκλήτους, non vocatos, satis indicat illos nequidem rogandos esse ut Deum pro nobis precentur: quod est precationem relativam illis denegare, non vero tantum absolutam.
english: Nor can anyone say with Cardinal Perron that when Origen denies that angels are to be prayed to and invoked, he means the kind of prayer they call absolute, not the kind called relative, which is the only kind the Roman school says may be used toward angels.

Celsus himself, whom Origen is answering, did not think that angels, or daemons, as he calls them with Plato, were to be worshiped with supreme and absolute worship, but with a worship referred to the supreme God, whose servants they were. So against the Christians he argued that they should be invoked, not with absolute prayer, as if they were the first and highest givers of good things, but only with relative prayer, as those who obtain and dispense those goods under the supreme God.

Since Origen denies that they are to be invoked in the way Celsus and other pagan philosophers wanted, it is plain that, according to Origen, neither absolute nor relative invocation may be used toward them. Moreover, when Origen says they pray for us uncalled, without being summoned, he shows clearly enough that they are not even to be asked to pray to God for us. That denies them relative prayer, not merely absolute prayer.

source_text: LXIX. Itaque Origenes pulsatus Celsi objectionibus, quasi Christiani summi Dei Ministros, & Angelicas potestates contemnerent, & nullo honore prosequerentur, non alium honorem illis exhibendum esse concedit, quam eum qui consistit in laude & imitatione: Eos, inquit, praedicamus beatos, & bene loquimur de illis, quibus a Deo commissae sunt utilitates hominum, non tamen honorem Deo debitum his reddimus. Saepius jam citato libro adversus Celsum Philosophum octavo. Ac praeterea loco quem supra descripsimus ex libro quinto ejusdem operis, affirmat Angelos, quantum humana natura fert, nobis imitandos esse; idque satis fore ut beati illi Spiritus bene nobis velint, & pro nobis in omnibus satagant: sed nullibi, quod tamen ad ejus scopum maxime fecisset, & calumniam Ethnicorum plenius adhuc retudisset, memorat nos eorum orationes precibus ambire, aut quicquam eorum quae in Ecclesia Romana hodie usitata sunt, in eorum honorem fieri.
english: So Origen, pressed by Celsus's objections that Christians despised the servants of the supreme God and the angelic powers and gave them no honor at all, grants that no other honor is to be given them than the honor that consists in praise and imitation. "We call them blessed," he says, "and we speak well of those to whom God has entrusted the welfare of human beings, yet we do not give them the honor owed to God." (Against Celsus the Philosopher, book 8, cited several times already.)

In the passage from book 5 of the same work quoted above, he also states that we are to imitate the angels as far as human nature allows, and that this will be enough for those blessed spirits to wish us well and to take pains for us in everything. But nowhere does he mention that we solicit their prayers by praying to them, or that any of the things used in the Roman Church today are done in their honor, though that would have served his purpose best and would have refuted the pagan slander even more fully.

source_text: LXX. Proinde quum Origenes octavo illo adversus Celsum libro, insinuat quandam θεραπείαν, id est, honoris & observantiae speciem veris Dei Ministris, Gabrieli, Michaeli, caeterisque Angelis & Archangelis deberi, θεραπεία ista, juxta doctrinam Origenis, nullo modo constitui potest in quadam eorum adoratione, & invocatione, quae in solidum & indivisibiliter uni summo Deo deberi contendit: sed in illa beatitudinis, gloriae & sanctitatis agnitione & celebratione, & etiam obsequii & amoris erga Deum pia imitatione, quibus Sanctos Angelos colere nos posse fatetur.
english: So when Origen, in that eighth book against Celsus, suggests that a certain therapeia, that is, a kind of honor and respect, is owed to God's true servants, Gabriel, Michael, and the other angels and archangels, that therapeia, by Origen's own teaching, can in no way consist in adoring or invoking them, which he insists is owed entirely and undivided to the one supreme God. It consists in acknowledging and celebrating their blessedness, glory, and holiness, and in devoutly imitating their obedience and love toward God. These are the ways in which he admits we may honor the holy angels.
